Tech stocks were sharply lower late Thursday afternoon, with the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) falling 7.3% and the State Street SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF (XSD) dropping 10%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor index fell 10.4%.

In sector news, ING Bank sees potentially tighter data-center regulation following the Democratic Party's decisive victory in Tuesday's midterm elections. "State-level policy will be more important to watch, as action is politically and practically easier at this level," ING said in a report Thursday. "The most likely approach is targeted regulation, much of which is already emerging. This includes data center-related taxes, reduced tax incentives, environmental standards, and requirements for developers to bear relevant cost increases."

In corporate news, Microsoft (MSFT) declined to extend a contract at a Texas data center with Nscale ahead of the startup's planned initial public offering, Bloomberg reported. Microsoft is tightening its oversight of some data center projects from Nebius (NBIS), Iren (IREN) and Nscale, as the neocloud companies deal with delays, regulatory issues and high costs, Bloomberg reported separately. Microsoft shares were down 3.9%, Nebius dropped 14%, and IREN shed 14%.

Qualcomm (QCOM) shares fell over 7% after its fiscal Q1 adjusted earnings forecast midpoint narrowly missed analysts' estimates, while Q4 earnings and revenue fell year-over-year.

Nvidia (NVDA) H200 chips are stacking up in Hong Kong as China holds off approval for large-volume shipments to the mainland, Reuters reported. Shares were down 9.1%.

Micron Technology (MU) has paused construction of its planned memory chip plant in Taiwan's Taoyuan City amid a prolonged labor dispute and uncertainty surrounding its agreement with a local union, Bloomberg reported. Shares were falling past 15%.

title: dYdX Team’s Arcus Opens Stock-Token Collateral to All Perps Traders, With a $20,000 Cap
detail:
dYdX Team’s Arcus Opens Stock-Token Collateral to All Perps Traders, With a $20,000 Cap
Arcus opens stock-token collateral to all perps traders
Unchained

WETH-USD
USDG33793-USD
QQQ
AAPL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Arcus, the Robinhood Chain exchange developed by the team that built dYdX, has opened Multi-Asset Collateral to every trader with access to its perpetual futures, removing the trading-volume requirement that had limited the feature since October. The company announced the change on Thursday.

As in early access, Arcus caps deposits of assets other than USDG at $20,000 per user and $2 million across the platform. Each account can borrow at most $10,000, according to Arcus's public lending data, and the exchange rejects orders that would push a loan past that limit. By Unchained's math, 100 traders depositing the $20,000 maximum would fill the platform-wide cap.

Traders can now back perps positions with ether, held as wrapped ether (WETH), and nine stock tokens alongside USDG, which most Arcus traders had needed for perps margin until now. The stock tokens are SPY, QQQ, Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta and Tesla, the last seven of which the press release groups as "MAG7." Each asset carries a 50% initial loan-to-value ratio.

Get Unchained's crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter.

Early Access Began Oct. 19

Arcus started rolling out the feature on Oct. 19 to accounts with more than $25 million in trading volume on the exchange, with the same assets and the same 50% ratio. Other traders do not need to switch anything on, according to Thursday's post.

How the Loans Work

The borrowing is automatic: once tokens sit in the perps account, any margin or losses the trader's USDG doesn't cover become a variable-rate loan that shrinks as the margin need falls. That rate was 4.94% a year on Thursday, according to Arcus's public lending feed. If falling token prices or a growing loan push the account past a maintenance level set for each asset, or the loan exceeds the per-account cap, Arcus can liquidate it, closing perps positions, selling the tokens, or both.

"Spot positions and perpetuals positions shouldn't have to operate in separate silos," founder and CEO Eddie Zhang said in the press release. He said the feature lets traders put stock token value to work "whether they're looking to maintain an existing position, put on a new trade or hedge their exposure."

Arcus, in which Robinhood Crypto is a strategic investor, is not available in the U.S., Canada or the U.K. The exchange launched leveraged stock and crypto tokens in August, and Robinhood Wallet began routing stock token trades through it on Oct. 1.

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) shares fell 2.59% to $541.39 at 10:35 a.m. ET in November 5 regular trading. The cloud and software giant's pullback puts the spotlight on a bigger question: how quickly can its AI buildout turn into durable profits and cash? Its October 28 results offer investors an operating benchmark as they track the trading session and weigh the returns on infrastructure spending.

The company's earnings release also separates OpenAI investment effects from non-GAAP earnings, helping investors distinguish operating performance from investment-related swings. With cloud generating more than two-thirds of revenue, the cost of supplying AI capacity carries substantial weight.

The GuruFocus snapshot shows a perfect GF Score of 100/100 and a price-to-earnings ratio of 28.27. Its radar chart signals broad strength across profitability, growth, valuation and momentum, with financial strength comparatively lower. Those readings support a strong business-quality assessment, but they cannot settle the AI spending debate. The next test is whether Microsoft can fill new capacity profitably and turn cloud demand into cash. Slower infrastructure investment could ease spending pressure while also limiting the capacity available to generate revenue.

Why Microsoft Stock is Down Today
Nauman Khan

Trading disclosure

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) shares fell 1.5% Thursday morning as investors weighed the company's decision not to increase its existing data center agreement with AI infrastructure provider Nscale in Texas.

The move leaves the current arrangement unchanged but ends the possibility of an expansion that could have added tens of billions of dollars to Nscale's business. Microsoft made the decision several months ago, before Nscale filed for an initial public offering in September, a person familiar with the matter said.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 5 Warning Sign with MSFT.

Is MSFT fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

MSFT GF Value chart

The existing commitment remains substantial. Nscale's IPO filing disclosed that work orders signed with Microsoft between September 2025 and April 2026 could generate up to $43.8 billion through December 2033, excluding optional extensions. The decision does not alter Nscale's reported contract value of about $103 billion, the source said.

Microsoft and Nscale had previously agreed to deploy roughly 200,000 Nvidia AI chips across data centers in the U.S. and Europe. The latest development follows Microsoft's withdrawal from a separate project in Loughton, England, after power connection delays pushed expected availability into the 2030s.

Nscale is seeking other customers for its Texas capacity, with Anthropic among the potential buyers.

title: Neocloud Stocks Fell More Than Hyperscalers After Election Night. Here's Why Exposure Differs.
detail:
Neocloud Stocks Fell More Than Hyperscalers After Election Night. Here's Why Exposure Differs.
Leo Sun, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 5, 2026 at 9:50 AM PST 5 min read
MSFT
CRWV
NVDA
AMZN
NBIS
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

On Nov. 3, the Democrats swept the House and Senate in the U.S. midterm elections. They also flipped the governorships of five states -- Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas -- from red to blue. That outcome was grim news for the booming AI market, since many Democrats support tighter restrictions on the construction of new data centers.

That's why it wasn't surprising when many top neocloud stocks -- including CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) and Nebius (NASDAQ: NBIS) -- dropped after election night. Yet the top hyperscaler stocks -- Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) -- rallied. Let's see why that happened, and if that divergence will continue for the foreseeable future.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Why did the neocloud stocks stumble?

Neocloud companies buy and lease data centers, load them up with Nvidia's top-tier GPUs, and rent that computing power to other companies. By providing only raw GPU power, these companies can process AI tasks more efficiently than larger cloud infrastructure platforms, such as Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure.

However, most of these neocloud companies are unprofitable, yet they're taking on more debt and issuing more shares to buy or lease new data centers and GPUs. That strategy works as long as the AI market continues to expand, regulators don't actively block the construction of new data centers, and interest rates remain stable.

But today, the macro headwinds could drive more companies to rein in their AI spending; the Democrats (and some Republicans) could actively block new data center projects, and the Fed -- which already raised its benchmark rates for the first time in three years this September -- could implement more rate hikes if inflation doesn't cool off.

CoreWeave, Nebius, and other neocloud companies are still growing rapidly, but they're racking up steep losses and taking on significant leverage.

CoreWeave ended the second quarter of 2026 with $72 billion in total liabilities, a debt-to-equity ratio of 14.3, and an average yield to maturity of 14.1% to 15.6% on its senior unsecured bonds. Analysts still expect its revenue to surge 151% in 2026 and 106% in 2027, but they're probably not sure if it can stay solvent if interest rates keep rising and the AI market cools off.
